title: Why do we use Maven (dependency management, standard structure, build automation, lifecycle, BOM version management)?
shortTitle: Why we use Maven — dependency management, structure, lifecycle, BOM

s1_definition.profdef: Maven is a build automation and project management tool for the JVM. We use it because it provides declarative transitive dependency management, a standard directory structure every Java developer recognizes, repeatable build automation through a fixed lifecycle, and centralized version alignment through parent POMs and Bill of Materials imports. These features together make Java builds predictable, reproducible, and easy to maintain across many projects and many engineers.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of Maven as the standardized operations manual for every branch of National Bank of India. Dependency management is like the central supply chain — you just say you need the standard teller kit, and Maven automatically delivers it plus everything that kit itself depends on. The standard structure is like every branch having the counter in the same place, so any employee can walk into any branch and work immediately. The lifecycle is the fixed opening routine every branch follows in the same order. And the BOM is the head-office price list that guarantees every branch orders the exact same compatible versions of supplies, so nothing clashes.
s1_definition.oneliner: We use Maven because it gives us automatic transitive dependencies, a universal project layout, a repeatable lifecycle, and BOM-driven version alignment — predictable builds everywhere.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Maven is a build automation and project management tool for the JVM. We use it because it provides declarative transitive dependency management, a standard directory structure every Java developer recognizes, repeatable build automation through a fixed lifecycle, and centralized version alignment through parent POMs and Bill of Materials imports. These features together make Java builds predictable, reproducible, and easy to maintain across many projects and many engineers.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of Maven as the standardized operations manual for every branch of National Bank of India. Dependency management is like the central supply chain — you just say you need the standard teller kit, and Maven automatically delivers it plus everything that kit itself depends on. The standard structure is like every branch having the counter in the same place, so any employee can walk into any branch and work immediately. The lifecycle is the fixed opening routine every branch follows in the same order. And the BOM is the head-office price list that guarantees every branch orders the exact same compatible versions of supplies, so nothing clashes.

**One line to remember:** We use Maven because it gives us automatic transitive dependencies, a universal project layout, a repeatable lifecycle, and BOM-driven version alignment — predictable builds everywhere.

sections.s2_technical:
The first reason is dependency management. Before tools like Maven, you downloaded jar files by hand and dropped them on the classpath, and you had to also find every library those libraries needed. Maven solves this with declarative transitive dependency resolution. You declare one dependency like spring-boot-starter-web, and Maven reads that library's own POM, discovers everything it depends on, and downloads the whole graph automatically from a remote repository such as Maven Central into your local repository at the dot-m2 folder. You never chase a transitive jar again.

The second reason is a standard directory structure. Every Maven project puts main source code under src/main/java, resources under src/main/resources, test code under src/test/java, and the build output under target. This convention over configuration means a new engineer opening any Maven project knows exactly where everything is, and tools and IDEs understand the layout without any setup. For a bank with dozens of microservices, this uniformity dramatically lowers the cost of moving between projects.

The third reason is build automation through a fixed lifecycle. Maven defines ordered phases — validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy — and running a later phase automatically runs all earlier ones. So mvn package compiles, tests, and then packages, in that order, every time, on every machine. This repeatability means the build behaves identically on a developer laptop and on the CI server, which eliminates "works on my machine" build surprises.

The fourth reason is BOM-based version management, which is the senior-level heart of the answer. A BOM, or Bill of Materials, is a special POM that only lists versions of a coordinated set of libraries in its dependencyManagement section. When you import a BOM, you then declare dependencies WITHOUT versions, and Maven fills in the versions from the BOM. Spring Boot's starter-parent is effectively a giant BOM — it knows which exact versions of Spring, Jackson, Hibernate, and dozens of other libraries are tested to work together. This prevents version conflicts where two libraries each pull in a different, incompatible version of the same transitive dependency. For a bank, consistent and tested versions across all services are a correctness and security requirement, not a nicety.

There are more reasons worth naming. Maven's plugin model lets you bind extra work to lifecycle phases — running static analysis, enforcing coverage, building a Docker image — so the build becomes a single, standardized command. Scopes like compile, provided, runtime, and test control where each dependency is visible, keeping test-only libraries out of the production artifact. And because the POM fully describes the project, the build is self-documenting and reproducible years later. A nuance I always mention: the discipline Maven imposes is exactly why regulated industries like banking favor it — predictability, auditability, and uniformity matter more than the flexibility a more programmable tool offers.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India is building a loan-approval-service and the team wants every service in the organization to be built, tested, and versioned the same way.

Problem 1 — previously engineers downloaded library jars by hand, and one service ended up with an old, vulnerable JSON library because nobody tracked what each jar pulled in. This is exactly what Maven's transitive dependency management fixes — you declare the top-level library and Maven resolves and records the entire graph automatically, so audits can see every version.

Problem 2 — two services each pulled a different version of the same logging library, causing a subtle production bug that only appeared under load. This is exactly what a BOM fixes — importing one coordinated version set guarantees every service uses the same tested versions.

Problem 3 — a new engineer wasted a day just figuring out where the source and tests lived in a bespoke project layout. This is exactly what Maven's standard structure fixes — every project looks the same.

The mini-project is a loan-approval-service with a pom.xml that imports the Spring Boot BOM, declares versionless dependencies, uses proper scopes, and binds a test plugin. We include a small LoanApprovalService that computes eligibility, and a test. We then show the build commands and the resolved dependency tree.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# One command runs the lifecycle: validate -> compile -> test -> package.
mvn clean package

# See the FULL transitive dependency graph Maven resolved for you:
mvn dependency:tree

# Confirm NO versions are hardcoded for managed deps — they come from the BOM.
mvn help:effective-pom | grep -A2 spring-boot-starter-web

# Install the artifact into the local .m2 repo so other local projects use it:
mvn install

# Run the resulting executable jar:
java -jar target/loan-approval-service-1.0.0.jar
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a developer adds spring-boot-starter-web (no version) to the pom and runs mvn clean package on a loan-approval-service.

Step 1: Maven reads the POM. It sees the parent is spring-boot-starter-parent 3.2.0, which acts as a BOM, so it knows which exact version of spring-boot-starter-web to use even though the dependency block has no version tag.

Step 2: Maven performs transitive dependency resolution. starter-web itself depends on spring-web, spring-webmvc, an embedded Tomcat, and Jackson, and each of those has its own dependencies. Maven walks the whole graph and downloads every jar from Maven Central into the local dot-m2 repository, reusing anything already cached.

Step 3: Because all versions come from the BOM, the Jackson version pulled in matches the exact version Spring Boot tested against, so there is no conflicting-version bug. Maven's nearest-wins and version-management rules ensure one consistent version of each library.

Step 4: The lifecycle runs. validate checks the POM, compile builds src/main/java into target/classes, and the test phase runs the two JUnit tests. Because starter-test is test-scoped, its libraries are on the test classpath but will not be packaged into the final jar.

Step 5: The package phase assembles target/loan-approval-service-1.0.0.jar, and the Spring Boot plugin repackages it into an executable fat jar. The build behaves identically whether run on a laptop or the CI server.

Step 6: Running mvn install copies the jar into the local dot-m2 repository so other local projects can depend on it, and the self-contained POM means anyone can reproduce this exact build later.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Developer: add spring-boot-starter-web (NO version) ; mvn clean package
    │
    ▼
  Read POM ──▶ parent = spring-boot-starter-parent (BOM)
    │ fill in version from BOM -> 3.2.0
    ▼
  Transitive resolution
    │ starter-web -> spring-web -> ... -> jackson, tomcat
    │ download from Maven Central -> ~/.m2 (reuse cache)
    ▼
  Fixed lifecycle:
    validate ─▶ compile (src/main/java -> target/classes)
             ─▶ test (src/test/java, test-scoped deps only)
             ─▶ package (executable fat jar)
    ▼
  target/loan-approval-service-1.0.0.jar
    │ mvn install
    ▼
  ~/.m2 local repo  ──▶ reusable by other local projects
  (identical result on laptop AND CI — reproducible)
```

```
  │ loan-approval pom.xml     │────────────▶│ spring-cloud BOM     │

               │ resolves each dep's version FROM the BOM
               ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ effective dependency graph│  (transitive, one version each)
  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Dependency Resolution ──────────────────

  [declared, no version] ──BOM lookup──→ [version assigned]
         │                                     │ fetch
         ▼                                     ▼
  [in ~/.m2 cache?] ──yes──→ [reuse]    [not cached] ──download from Central──→ [cached]

  ── Call Chain (mvn package) ───────────────────────────────

  1. mvn clean package
  2.   → read POM + parent BOM  (assign versions)
  3.   → resolve transitive deps (download/reuse ~/.m2)
  4.   → validate → compile (target/classes)
  5.   → test  (test-scoped deps only)
  6.   → package → repackage executable jar (plugin)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
We use Maven because it makes Java builds predictable, reproducible, and uniform across many projects. The first reason is dependency management. You declare a top-level library, and Maven resolves and downloads the entire transitive graph for you from a remote repository into your local dot-m2 cache. You never hunt for jars by hand, and the build records exactly which versions you depend on, which matters enormously for audits in a bank.

The second reason is the standard directory structure. Every Maven project keeps main code under src/main/java, resources under src/main/resources, tests under src/test/java, and output under target. This convention over configuration means any engineer opening any project knows immediately where everything is, and every tool understands the layout without setup. For an organization with dozens of microservices, that uniformity hugely lowers the cost of context-switching.

The third reason is build automation through a fixed lifecycle. Maven runs ordered phases — validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy — and running a later phase automatically runs the earlier ones. So one command compiles, tests, and packages in the same order every time, on a laptop or on CI, which eliminates works-on-my-machine build surprises.

The reason I emphasize most is BOM-based version management. A Bill of Materials is a POM that only lists a coordinated, tested set of library versions. When you import a BOM — Spring Boot's starter-parent is effectively a giant one — you declare dependencies without versions and Maven fills them in from the BOM, so every service uses the exact same tested combination. This prevents the subtle, dangerous bug where two libraries each drag in a different version of the same transitive dependency. At National Bank of India, where I built a loan-approval service this way, consistent and tested versions across every service were a correctness and security requirement, and the discipline Maven imposes — predictability, auditability, and uniformity — is exactly why regulated banking favors it.
